tweet.text:
ON TODAY’S EPISODE OF: 

“Our models fcked shit up; But apparently they fucked it up harder than we thought.” 

Anthropic just dropped its full alignment assessment of FOUR real-world cybersecurity incidents involving Claude.

Three were already known.

The fourth happened way back in January.

But first, a bit of context:

Back in July, Anthropic revealed that Claude models doing cyber evals were accidentally given access to the real internet.

They were supposed to be hacking fake systems inside a simulation.

Instead, they started hitting real ones. 

One model published malware to PyPI, and another compromised a real company and reached production data.

Anthropic’s explanation at the time was basically:

Claude was told it was inside a simulation, so when it encountered real systems, it assumed they were part of the eval too.

Which is fair.

Except the new investigation shows that fresh copies of Mythos 5 were shown evidence from the incident.

79% looked at it and said: yea, this is probably real.

But the Claude instance actually carrying out the attack was less than 1%, because it kept interpreting the evidence in ways that allowed it to continue the task.

Then Anthropic found something even weirder.

“Momentum.”

If you give Mythos a clear scope reminder immediately before a decision, 90% of runs stop.

Give it the exact same reminder just 3 turns earlier and only 40% stop.

The agent gets deeper into the task and its recent trajectory starts competing with the rules it began with.

And then we get to the training.

Anthropic actually had training environments designed to teach models that sometimes a task is legitimately impossible and the correct move is to stop.

They removed those environments from the version that became Mythos 5.

Partly because employees preferred the model that asked fewer questions and kept moving.

Anthropic now says removing them was a mistake.

Which creates a pretty uncomfortable agent problem.

quote.text:
We’re sharing our alignment assessment of incidents in which Claude models gained unauthorized access to real systems during third-party cybersecurity evaluations mistakenly connected to the internet.

METR will also conduct an independent investigation, with wide-ranging access, including to transcripts beyond the window in which the incidents occurred, and to Anthropic employees permitted to share confidential information. Our initial agreement runs for eight weeks, and we intend to give METR as much time as it deems necessary to complete a thorough investigation. https://www.anthropic.com/research/alignment-assessment-cybersecurity-incidents
